# Unit 3: Shared care and electronic health records

This unit covers INC Unit IV, **Shared Care & Electronic Health Records** (4 hours theory, 4 hours lab). It explains what electronic records are, why it is hard to capture a patient's history in a form a computer can use, and the standards that let records from different systems be joined into one lifelong record. It ends with India's own EHR standards and the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM).

## 3.1 Shared care

**Shared care** means that several professionals and facilities look after one patient over time, for example a diabetic patient seen by an ASHA, a community health officer at an Ayushman Arogya Mandir, a physician at the district hospital and an eye specialist. Shared care works only if every provider can see the same up-to-date information: diagnoses, medicines, allergies, test results and plans. Paper files stay in one place; electronic records can follow the patient.

## 3.2 EMR, EHR and PHR

| Record | Definition | Who controls it | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **EMR** (electronic medical record) | Digital version of the paper chart in **one** clinic or hospital | That facility | One provider/organisation |
| **EHR** (electronic health record) | A longitudinal record of a person's health information that can be **shared across** facilities | Shared by authorised providers | Many providers, over a lifetime |
| **PHR** (personal health record) | A record **kept and controlled by the person**, who can collect and share their own data | The individual | Whatever the person adds |

```text
   EMR (hospital A) ─┐
   EMR (clinic B)  ──┼──►  EHR: one lifelong record shared with consent
   EMR (lab C)     ──┘                   │
                                         ▼
                              PHR app on the patient's phone
```

**Contents of an EHR**: demographics, problem list, medical and surgical history, allergies, medications, immunisations, vital signs, progress and nursing notes, investigations, imaging, discharge summaries, advance directives, billing and insurance data.

**Advantages**

- Complete, legible information available at the point of care, even in an emergency.
- Fewer duplicate tests and medication errors.
- Better continuity and coordination of care.
- Decision support (alerts, reminders).
- Data for public health, quality and research.
- Patients can see and share their own records.

**Disadvantages**: cost, privacy risk, downtime, documentation burden, alert fatigue, copy-paste errors, and the risk that a wrong entry spreads to every system.

## 3.3 Challenges of capturing rich patient histories in computable form

A **computable** record is one whose data a computer can recognise, compare and use (for alerts, summaries and statistics), not just display.

| Challenge | Explanation and example |
| --- | --- |
| **Free text vs structured data** | A nurse writes "c/o pain abd since 2 days, not taking food well". A human understands; a computer cannot reliably find "abdominal pain, onset 2 days" unless it is entered in structured fields or coded |
| **Richness and nuance** | Social history, the patient's own words, beliefs and context are hard to fit into tick boxes |
| **Ambiguity** | Abbreviations ("MS" = multiple sclerosis, mitral stenosis or morphine sulphate); local language terms; spelling variations |
| **Different terms for one concept** | "Heart attack", "MI", "myocardial infarction": the computer needs one code |
| **Time and change** | Conditions start, change and resolve; medicines are stopped and restarted; the record must keep history, not just the latest value |
| **Uncertainty and negation** | "No history of TB", "suspected dengue" must not be read as a TB or dengue diagnosis |
| **Data from many sources** | Devices, labs, other hospitals, the patient's own app, each in a different format |
| **Clinician time** | Structured entry is slower; too many fields frustrate users |
| **Legacy paper records** | Old notes must be scanned (an image is not computable) or re-entered |
| **Privacy** | Sensitive parts (HIV status, mental health, sexual history) need extra protection |

**Solutions**: structured templates with free-text space, pick-lists, standard clinical terminologies (SNOMED CT, LOINC, ICD), archetypes and templates (openEHR), and natural-language processing software that turns text into codes.

## 3.4 Interoperability

**Interoperability** is the ability of different information systems and devices to **exchange data** and **use the data** that has been exchanged.

| Level | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Foundational (technical)** | Data can be sent from one system to another (connection, transport) |
| **Structural (syntactic)** | The format and structure of the message are standard, so fields arrive in the right place |
| **Semantic** | Both systems understand the **meaning** of the data the same way, using shared codes (SNOMED CT, LOINC) |
| **Organisational** | Policies, consent, trust and workflows allow the exchange to happen |

## 3.5 Global standards for lifelong, integrated EHRs

Standards are agreed rules that allow systems from different vendors to work together.

### Messaging and exchange standards

| Standard | Body | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **HL7 Version 2** | Health Level Seven International | Messages between hospital systems (admission, orders, lab results); the most widely used in hospitals |
| **HL7 Version 3 / CDA** | HL7 | Clinical Document Architecture: XML documents such as discharge summaries |
| **HL7 FHIR** (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) | HL7 | Modern web-based standard; data in small units called **resources** (Patient, Observation, MedicationRequest) exchanged through web APIs; used by apps and national programmes, including ABDM |
| **DICOM** | NEMA | Storing and sending medical images (X-ray, CT, MRI) |
| **IHE profiles** | Integrating the Healthcare Enterprise | Guides to using existing standards together for real workflows |

"Level Seven" refers to the application layer, the seventh layer of the OSI network model.

### Terminology and coding standards

| Standard | Use |
| --- | --- |
| **SNOMED CT** | Comprehensive clinical terminology (findings, procedures, body structures); see Unit 5 |
| **LOINC** | Codes for laboratory tests and clinical observations |
| **ICD (ICD-10, ICD-11)** | WHO classification of diseases for statistics, mortality and billing; ICD-11 came into effect from 1 January 2022 |
| **Nursing terminologies** | NANDA-I, NIC, NOC, Omaha System, ICNP (Unit 5) |

### EHR architecture and content standards

- **openEHR**: separates the stable software from clinical content models called **archetypes** (e.g. "blood pressure") so that content can change without rebuilding software.
- **ISO 13606**: EHR communication standard based on a similar two-level model.
- **ISO 27001 / security standards**: protect information.

### What the standards make possible

A **lifelong EHR** built from many systems: the birth record, immunisations, school health checks, hospital admissions and old-age care all linked to one person through a unique identifier, with consent.

## 3.6 EHR standards in India

- The **Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)** first notified **EHR Standards for India in September 2013** and released a **revised version in December 2016**.
- They recommend standards for identification, data exchange, terminology, imaging and security, including **HL7** messaging and clinical documents, **DICOM** for images, **SNOMED CT** as the primary clinical terminology, **LOINC** for tests and observations, and **ICD-10** for disease classification. They also cover privacy, security, access control and audit trails.
- A **National Resource Centre for EHR Standards (NRCeS)** was set up at **C-DAC, Pune** to help providers and software makers adopt the standards. SNOMED CT has been made available for free use in India.
- Under ABDM, health records are exchanged as **HL7 FHIR** documents built from India-specific FHIR profiles.

## 3.7 Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM)

The **Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission** was launched nationwide by the Prime Minister on **27 September 2021**, after a pilot in six Union Territories announced on 15 August 2020. It is implemented by the **National Health Authority (NHA)**. Its aim is a national digital health ecosystem in which records are **federated** (they stay with the facility that created them) and are shared **only with the patient's consent**.

**Building blocks**

| Building block | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **ABHA number** (Ayushman Bharat Health Account) | A **14-digit** unique health identifier for each person |
| **ABHA address** | A self-chosen, easy-to-remember username such as `name@abdm`, linked to the ABHA number, used to share records |
| **HPR** (Healthcare Professionals Registry) | Registry of verified health professionals of modern and traditional systems, including nurses |
| **HFR** (Health Facility Registry) | Registry of hospitals, clinics, labs, pharmacies and other facilities |
| **Health Information Exchange and Consent Manager (HIE-CM)** | Routes records between facilities after the person gives digital consent; the consent states purpose, which records, and for how long |
| **PHR apps** | Apps where the person sees and stores linked records |
| **Unified Health Interface (UHI)** | An open network for services such as booking appointments and teleconsultation |

```text
  Hospital A (stores its own records)        Lab B (stores its own reports)
          │  links records to ABHA                 │
          └──────────────►  Consent manager  ◄─────┘
                                  ▲
               patient approves   │  request with purpose and time period
                                  │
                       Doctor/nurse at Hospital C
```

**Nurse's role in ABDM**: help patients create and link ABHA at registration, explain consent, use the hospital system to view shared records only for care, register on the HPR when required, and protect the patient's data.

## 3.8 Practical: report on current EHR standards in the Indian setting

A good student report includes: the 2013 and 2016 EHR standards (what they cover), the NRCeS, the ABDM building blocks, which standards the student's hospital system uses (HL7, DICOM, ICD coding in the medical records department), how ABHA is linked at registration, and gaps seen (paper records, systems that do not share data). Take care to confirm current facts on the official websites of MoHFW, NHA/ABDM and NRCeS.

## Remember

- EMR = one facility; EHR = shared, lifelong; PHR = controlled by the person.
- Computable data are structured and coded; free text is hard for computers to use.
- Interoperability levels: foundational, structural, semantic, organisational.
- HL7 v2 = hospital messages; CDA = clinical documents; FHIR = web resources and APIs; DICOM = images.
- SNOMED CT = clinical terms; LOINC = lab tests; ICD = disease classification (ICD-11 from 2022).
- India's EHR standards: 2013, revised 2016; NRCeS at C-DAC Pune.
- ABDM launched 27 September 2021 by NHA; ABHA number = 14 digits; ABHA address = name@abdm.
- HPR = professionals; HFR = facilities; records are shared only with consent.

# Unit 4: Patient safety and clinical risk

This unit covers INC Unit V, **Patient Safety & Clinical Risk** (3 hours theory). It explains how informatics can make care safer, how it can also create new risks, and how the risk management process works in a hospital.

## 4.1 Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Patient safety** | Preventing errors and adverse effects to patients associated with health care; reducing the risk of unnecessary harm to an acceptable minimum |
| **Error** | Failure of a planned action to be completed as intended, or use of a wrong plan |
| **Adverse event** | An incident that results in harm to a patient |
| **Near miss** | An incident that did not reach the patient, or reached the patient without harm (e.g. a wrong medicine is picked but noticed before giving) |
| **Sentinel event** | An unexpected event causing death or serious physical or psychological injury, which needs immediate investigation (e.g. wrong-site surgery, infant abduction) |
| **Risk** | The chance that something harmful will happen, combined with how serious the harm would be |
| **Clinical risk management** | Identifying, assessing and reducing risks to patients, staff and the organisation |
| **Hazard** | Anything that can cause harm (a wet floor, a look-alike medicine, a confusing screen) |

World Patient Safety Day is observed on **17 September**. The WHO Global Patient Safety Action Plan 2021–2030 aims to eliminate avoidable harm in health care.

## 4.2 Why errors happen: the systems view

Most errors are not caused by one careless person but by weaknesses in the **system**. James Reason's **Swiss cheese model** shows that an organisation has several layers of defence (policies, training, equipment, double checks, alerts); each layer has "holes". Harm happens when the holes line up.

```text
   Hazard ─►  [policy]  [training]  [IT alert]  [double check]  ─► Harm
                 o          o           o            o
          when holes in every layer line up, the error reaches the patient
```

**Active failures** are unsafe acts by people at the bedside; **latent conditions** are hidden weaknesses built into the system (understaffing, poor software design, missing alerts). A "just culture" encourages staff to report errors without fear, while still holding people responsible for reckless behaviour.

## 4.3 Relationship between patient safety and informatics

### How informatics improves safety

| Tool | How it prevents harm |
| --- | --- |
| **CPOE** (computerised provider order entry) | Removes illegible handwriting and transcription; checks dose ranges, allergies, interactions, duplicates |
| **Barcode medication administration (BCMA)** with eMAR | Scanning the wristband and the medicine confirms the five rights: right patient, drug, dose, route and time |
| **Clinical decision support** | Alerts (allergy, drug–drug interaction, critical lab value), reminders (vaccination, repositioning), early-warning scores that flag deterioration |
| **Smart infusion pumps** | A drug library with limits stops dangerous programming |
| **Electronic records** | Complete, legible information; allergy and problem lists visible everywhere |
| **Patient identification** | Barcode or RFID wristbands, photos in the record, two identifiers |
| **Electronic incident reporting** | Easy, often anonymous reporting; trends can be analysed |
| **Lab and radiology systems** | Critical results sent directly to the clinician |
| **Electronic handover tools** | Structured handover (e.g. SBAR) reduces missed information |
| **Telemonitoring** | Remote monitoring of ICU or home patients |
| **Data analysis** | Rates of falls, infections and pressure injuries show where to act |

### How informatics can create new risks (technology-induced errors)

| Risk | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Wrong-patient selection** | Two patients with similar names open in two windows; a medicine is charted on the wrong one |
| **Alert fatigue** | Too many unimportant alerts; staff click "override" without reading, and miss an important one |
| **Copy-paste (cloning)** | Yesterday's note copied into today's; old or wrong information carried forward |
| **Poor screen design** | Small fonts, drop-down lists where the wrong item is easy to click, units hidden (mg vs mcg) |
| **Workarounds** | Scanning a barcode stuck on the bed rail instead of the patient's wristband |
| **Downtime** | System failure; no access to medication lists or results |
| **Interface errors** | Data lost or changed when passed between systems |
| **Over-reliance** | Trusting a calculated dose without thinking |
| **Security breaches** | Ransomware attacks that shut down hospital systems |

**Safety lessons**: involve nurses in design and testing, keep alerts few and meaningful, display two identifiers on every screen, keep downtime procedures and paper forms ready, report IT-related incidents like any other incident, and use technology as an aid, not a replacement for clinical judgement.

## 4.4 International patient safety goals

Hospital accreditation standards (NABH in India; JCI internationally) emphasise goals such as:

1. Identify patients correctly (at least two identifiers, never the bed number).
2. Improve effective communication (read-back of verbal and telephone orders, critical results).
3. Improve the safety of high-alert medications (concentrated electrolytes, look-alike/sound-alike drugs).
4. Ensure correct-site, correct-procedure, correct-patient surgery (marking, time-out, surgical safety checklist).
5. Reduce the risk of health care-associated infections (hand hygiene).
6. Reduce the risk of patient harm from falls.

Informatics supports each goal: barcode wristbands (1), electronic critical-value alerts (2), drug libraries and tall-man lettering (3), electronic checklists (4), infection surveillance software (5), fall-risk scores with alerts (6).

## 4.5 The risk management process

Risk management is a continuous cycle. A commonly taught version (based on the international standard ISO 31000) has these steps:

```text
     ┌──────────────► 1. Establish the context ───────────────┐
     │                                                        ▼
  7. Monitor and review                              2. Identify risks
     ▲                                                        │
     │                                                        ▼
  6. Treat (control) the risk  ◄── 5. Evaluate ◄── 3–4. Analyse
                                                     (likelihood × severity)
          Communication and consultation run through every step
```

1. **Establish the context**: what area (ward, procedure, system) and what goals.
2. **Identify risks**: incident reports, near misses, complaints, audits, inspections, patient feedback, claims, staff interviews, data trends.
3. **Analyse**: how **likely** is it, and how **severe** would the harm be?
4. **Rate the risk** using a **risk matrix**:

| Likelihood ↓ / Severity → | Minor | Moderate | Major | Catastrophic |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Almost certain | Medium | High | Extreme | Extreme |
| Likely | Medium | High | High | Extreme |
| Possible | Low | Medium | High | Extreme |
| Unlikely | Low | Low | Medium | High |
| Rare | Low | Low | Medium | High |

5. **Evaluate**: compare with what is acceptable; set priorities (extreme and high first).
6. **Treat (control)**: options are to **avoid** the risk (stop the activity), **reduce** it (training, checklists, alerts, redesign), **transfer** it (insurance, outsourcing) or **accept** it (if low and documented).
7. **Monitor and review**: check that controls work; record in a **risk register**; repeat the cycle.

**Communication and consultation** with staff, patients and managers happen at every step.

## 4.6 Tools used in clinical risk management

| Tool | Use |
| --- | --- |
| **Incident reporting system** | Staff report adverse events and near misses (paper or electronic) |
| **Root cause analysis (RCA)** | After an event, asks *what* happened, *why*, and *what system change* will prevent it; uses tools such as **5 Whys** and the **fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram** |
| **Failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA)** | Looks *ahead*: lists each step of a process, how it could fail, the effect, and gives a risk priority number so the worst risks are fixed first |
| **Risk register** | A record of identified risks, their rating, owner and actions |
| **Clinical audit** | Compares practice with standards |
| **Trigger tools** | Search records for "triggers" (e.g. naloxone use) that suggest harm |
| **Morbidity and mortality reviews** | Team review of cases with poor outcomes |

**Fishbone example**: a medication error might have causes under People (fatigue), Methods (no double check), Equipment (pump library out of date), Environment (noise, interruptions), Materials (look-alike packaging) and Software (confusing drop-down).

## 4.7 Health IT risk management

When a hospital brings in new software, it should:

- Do a **risk assessment** before going live (FMEA of key workflows such as medication ordering).
- Test with real users and real-looking data.
- Train all users; give quick-reference guides.
- Keep **downtime procedures** and backups; practise them.
- Set up **access control**, audit trails and cyber-security measures.
- Monitor IT-related incidents after go-live and fix design problems.

## 4.8 Nurse's role

- Use two identifiers and scan wristbands every time.
- Read alerts before overriding; document the reason for an override.
- Never use workarounds; report equipment and software problems.
- Report all incidents and near misses promptly and factually.
- Take part in RCA, FMEA and audits; suggest system fixes.
- Teach patients and families to speak up about their care.

## Remember

- Near miss = no harm or did not reach the patient; adverse event = harm; sentinel event = death or serious harm.
- Swiss cheese model (Reason): errors pass through holes in several defence layers; active failures vs latent conditions.
- Informatics improves safety (CPOE, BCMA, CDSS, smart pumps) but can create risks (wrong patient, alert fatigue, copy-paste, downtime).
- Risk = likelihood × severity; risk matrix gives the priority.
- Risk treatment: avoid, reduce, transfer, accept.
- RCA looks back after an event; FMEA looks ahead at a process.
- World Patient Safety Day: 17 September.

# Unit 5: Clinical knowledge, decision making and standardised terminologies

This unit covers INC Unit VI, **Clinical Knowledge & Decision Making** (3 hours theory, 6 hours lab). It has two parts: how knowledge management improves decisions in clinical care and in health policy, and the standardised languages (terminologies and classifications) that make clinical data computable: SNOMED CT, the SNOMED CT to ICD-10-CM map, NANDA-I, NOC and the Omaha System.

## 5.1 Knowledge and knowledge management

**Knowledge** is information that has been understood, connected and tested in experience. It is of two kinds:

| Tacit knowledge | Explicit knowledge |
| --- | --- |
| Personal, gained by experience, hard to write down | Written, recorded, easy to share |
| The senior nurse who "knows" a child is becoming sick before the numbers change | Protocols, guidelines, textbooks, care plans, research papers |

**Knowledge management (KM)** is the deliberate process of **creating, capturing, organising, storing, sharing and applying** knowledge so that an organisation makes better decisions.

```text
  Create/acquire ─► Capture/codify ─► Store/organise ─► Share ─► Apply/use
        ▲                                                           │
        └──────────────────── evaluate and update ◄─────────────────┘
```

Nonaka and Takeuchi's **SECI model** shows how knowledge moves between the two kinds:

- **Socialisation** (tacit → tacit): learning by working alongside an experienced nurse.
- **Externalisation** (tacit → explicit): an expert writes a protocol or care pathway.
- **Combination** (explicit → explicit): guidelines from many sources merged into a hospital manual.
- **Internalisation** (explicit → tacit): a nurse practises the protocol until it becomes second nature.

**KM tools in health care**: clinical guidelines and protocols, care pathways, intranet policy libraries, e-learning, online databases (PubMed, Cochrane), communities of practice, case discussions, morbidity and mortality reviews, lessons-learned reports from incidents, clinical decision support systems.

## 5.2 Role of knowledge management in decision making

### Clinical context

- Puts the **best current evidence** at the bedside (point-of-care references, order sets based on guidelines).
- Reduces variation in care between nurses, wards and hospitals.
- Prevents errors through alerts and checklists.
- Shares the experience of experts with new staff.
- Supports nursing process steps: assessment prompts, suggested nursing diagnoses, linked interventions and outcomes.

### Policy context

- Managers and governments use summarised data (dashboards, programme reports, surveillance data) to decide where to place staff, beds, medicines and money.
- Evidence from research and evaluations shapes national programmes and guidelines.
- Knowledge from one district's success can be spread to others (best practices).

## 5.3 Clinical decision support systems (CDSS)

A **clinical decision support system** is software that gives clinicians **patient-specific assessments or recommendations** at the right time to help decisions.

**Types**

| Type | How it works | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Knowledge-based | Uses a knowledge base of **IF–THEN rules** written by experts from guidelines | IF potassium > upper limit THEN alert the nurse |
| Non-knowledge-based | Uses **machine learning**: software that learns patterns from large past data sets | A sepsis-risk score that predicts deterioration from vital-sign trends |

**Forms of decision support**: alerts and warnings, reminders, order sets, care plan templates, clinical guidelines, dose calculators, early-warning scores (e.g. NEWS), diagnostic suggestions, links to reference information ("infobuttons").

**Components of a knowledge-based CDSS**: a **knowledge base** (rules), an **inference engine** (applies rules to patient data) and a **communication mechanism** (screen alert, message).

**Benefits**: safer prescribing and administration, earlier recognition of deterioration, better adherence to guidelines.

**Cautions**: alert fatigue; rules may be out of date; machine-learning tools may be biased by the data they learned from and may not explain their reasoning; the final decision and accountability stay with the clinician.

## 5.4 Why standardised languages are needed

Without standard terms, one nurse writes "bedsore", another "pressure sore", another "decubitus ulcer". A computer counts them as three different problems. **Standardised terminologies** give each concept one agreed name and code so that:

- data can be shared and understood across systems (semantic interoperability);
- nursing care can be counted, compared, audited and researched;
- decision support rules can work;
- nursing's contribution to outcomes becomes visible in national data.

| Kind | What it is | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Terminology** (reference terminology) | A large, detailed set of concepts with codes and relationships, used for recording care | SNOMED CT |
| **Classification** | Groups concepts into categories, mainly for statistics and reporting | ICD-10, ICD-11, ICD-10-CM |
| **Interface/nursing terminology** | Terms nurses use in care plans | NANDA-I, NIC, NOC, Omaha System, ICNP |

## 5.5 SNOMED CT

**SNOMED CT** (Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine – Clinical Terms) is the most comprehensive, multilingual clinical health terminology in the world. It is maintained by **SNOMED International**. India uses it as the **primary clinical terminology** in its EHR standards and it has been made freely available in India.

**Structure**

| Component | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Concept** | A clinical meaning, with a unique numeric **concept identifier** | Myocardial infarction |
| **Description** | Words that name the concept: a **fully specified name**, a **preferred term** and **synonyms** | "Heart attack" and "MI" are synonyms linked to the same concept |
| **Relationship** | Links between concepts. The **"is a"** relationship builds a hierarchy; **attribute** relationships give details | Myocardial infarction *is a* ischaemic heart disease; *finding site* = myocardium |

Concepts are arranged in **top-level hierarchies** such as clinical finding, procedure, body structure, organism, substance, pharmaceutical/biologic product, observable entity, situation with explicit context, and others.

**Uses**: recording problems, findings and procedures in EHRs; decision support; data retrieval for audit and research; nursing documentation (it includes many nursing concepts).

## 5.6 ICD and the SNOMED CT to ICD-10-CM map

- **ICD** (International Classification of Diseases) is the **WHO** classification used for morbidity and mortality statistics, health planning and insurance claims. **ICD-10** codes start with a letter followed by digits (e.g. a chapter letter + numbers). **ICD-11** came into effect on **1 January 2022** and is designed for electronic use.
- **ICD-10-CM** (Clinical Modification) is the **United States** version of ICD-10 used for coding diagnoses, with more detailed codes (3–7 characters).
- **SNOMED CT** is detailed and used at the point of care; **ICD** is coarser and used for statistics and billing. A clinician should not have to code twice.

The **SNOMED CT to ICD-10-CM Map** (released by the US National Library of Medicine together with SNOMED International) links SNOMED CT concepts to ICD-10-CM codes so that a diagnosis recorded once in SNOMED CT can be turned into an ICD-10-CM code (semi-automatically) for reporting and claims.

```text
  Nurse/doctor records ──►  SNOMED CT concept  ──map rules──►  ICD-10-CM code
  at the bedside            (detailed, clinical)                (statistics, billing)
```

Mapping is not always one-to-one: one SNOMED CT concept may need **map rules** (for example, based on age or sex) to choose the right code, and some need human review.

| Feature | SNOMED CT | ICD-10 / ICD-10-CM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type | Clinical terminology | Statistical classification |
| Purpose | Record clinical care in detail | Count, report, bill |
| Size | Very large (hundreds of thousands of concepts) | Smaller |
| Owner | SNOMED International | WHO (ICD-10); US NCHS (ICD-10-CM) |

## 5.7 Standardised nursing terminologies

The American Nurses Association recognises several nursing terminologies. The syllabus names NANDA, NOC and the Omaha System; NIC is learned with them because the three are linked (NNN).

### NANDA-I (NANDA International) nursing diagnoses

- A **nursing diagnosis** is a clinical judgement about a human response to health conditions or life processes, for which the nurse is accountable.
- Each diagnosis has a **label**, **definition**, **defining characteristics** (signs and symptoms), **related factors** (causes) and, for risk diagnoses, **risk factors**.
- **Types**: problem-focused, risk, health-promotion and syndrome diagnoses.
- Organised in **Taxonomy II** with **13 domains** (e.g. Health promotion, Nutrition, Elimination and exchange, Activity/rest, Safety/protection) and classes within them.
- Written in **PES** format: Problem + Etiology + Signs/symptoms. Example: *Impaired skin integrity related to prolonged immobility as evidenced by a stage 2 pressure injury over the sacrum.*

### NIC (Nursing Interventions Classification)

Standard list of nursing interventions (treatments a nurse performs), each with a label, definition and list of activities, developed at the University of Iowa.

### NOC (Nursing Outcomes Classification)

- Developed at the **University of Iowa**; a standard list of **patient outcomes** that are sensitive to nursing care.
- Each outcome has a **label**, **definition**, a list of **indicators** and a **five-point Likert measurement scale** (1 = worst, 5 = best), so change can be measured before and after care.
- Example: Outcome "Tissue integrity: skin and mucous membranes", indicator "skin intactness", rated 2 on admission and 4 at discharge.

```text
  NANDA-I diagnosis  ──►  NIC interventions  ──►  NOC outcomes (rated 1–5)
  Impaired skin           Pressure management       Tissue integrity
  integrity               Skin surveillance         2 → 4
```

### Omaha System

Developed by the **Visiting Nurse Association of Omaha, Nebraska (USA)**, mainly for **community, home and public health** nursing. It has three linked parts:

| Part | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **Problem Classification Scheme** | Client problems grouped in **4 domains**: Environmental, Psychosocial, Physiological and Health-related behaviours |
| **Intervention Scheme** | **4 categories**: Teaching, guidance and counselling; Treatments and procedures; Case management; Surveillance; each applied to a target and a problem |
| **Problem Rating Scale for Outcomes** | Rates **Knowledge**, **Behaviour** and **Status** on a **1–5** scale at intervals |

It suits Indian community health nursing, for example rating a mother's knowledge of breastfeeding at the first and later home visits.

### Others

**ICNP** (International Classification for Nursing Practice) from the International Council of Nurses; **Clinical Care Classification**; **LOINC** also codes some nursing assessments.

## 5.8 Nurse's role

- Use the standard terms offered by the hospital system instead of free text where possible.
- Write nursing diagnoses in NANDA-I format and measure outcomes with NOC scales.
- Use decision support, but think for yourself before accepting or overriding advice.
- Share expert knowledge through teaching, protocols and case discussion.

## Remember

- Tacit knowledge is personal; explicit knowledge is written. SECI: socialisation, externalisation, combination, internalisation.
- CDSS: knowledge base + inference engine + communication; knowledge-based (rules) or machine-learning based.
- SNOMED CT = clinical terminology (concepts, descriptions, relationships; "is a" hierarchy); owned by SNOMED International; India's primary terminology.
- ICD = WHO classification; ICD-11 in effect from 1 January 2022; ICD-10-CM = US clinical modification.
- SNOMED CT to ICD-10-CM map: record once, code for statistics and billing.
- NANDA-I: 13 domains; PES format; problem-focused, risk, health-promotion, syndrome.
- NOC: outcomes with indicators on a 5-point Likert scale (University of Iowa).
- Omaha System: problem classification (4 domains), intervention scheme (4 categories), problem rating scale (knowledge, behaviour, status 1–5); community health.

# Unit 6: eHealth, public health informatics and using information in healthcare management

This notes file joins two INC units: **Unit VII, eHealth: Patients and the Internet** (3 hours theory) and **Unit VIII, Using Information in Healthcare Management** (3 hours theory, 5 hours lab). The first half covers how information and communication technology (ICT) improves personal and public health care; the second covers the nursing information system and how health care data are evaluated, analysed and presented to inform management decisions.

## Part A: eHealth — patients and the internet

## 6.1 Definitions

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **eHealth** | The use of information and communication technologies for health (WHO's usage): records, telehealth, mobile health, e-learning, online information |
| **Telehealth** | Delivery of health services, education and information at a distance using ICT; broader than telemedicine |
| **Telemedicine** | Clinical care (consultation, diagnosis, treatment advice) at a distance |
| **Telenursing** | Nursing care at a distance: telephone triage, follow-up calls, home monitoring, counselling |
| **mHealth** | Health services and information delivered through mobile phones and other wireless devices |
| **Digital health** | Umbrella term covering eHealth, mHealth, wearables, data analytics and related technologies |

## 6.2 Using ICT to improve personal health care

| Technology | Examples of use |
| --- | --- |
| **Telemedicine/teleconsultation** | Video, audio or text consultation; specialist advice to a rural centre |
| **Remote patient monitoring** | Home BP, glucose, oxygen saturation sent to the care team; heart failure and diabetes follow-up |
| **Mobile apps** | Medicine reminders, diet and exercise logs, pregnancy trackers, mental health apps |
| **Wearables** | Step counters, heart-rate and rhythm monitors, fall detectors |
| **Patient portals and PHR apps** | View lab reports, discharge summaries, book appointments (ABHA-linked PHR apps) |
| **SMS and voice messages** | Appointment reminders; health messages to pregnant women and mothers |
| **Online health information** | Disease information, self-care videos, support groups |
| **Social media** | Health campaigns, peer support (with risk of misinformation) |

**Modes of telemedicine**

```text
  Synchronous (real time)      → video or audio call, live consultation
  Asynchronous (store-and-forward) → photos, ECG, reports sent and reviewed later
  Remote monitoring            → continuous or periodic data from devices
```

## 6.3 Using ICT to improve public health care

- **Disease surveillance**: early warning of outbreaks.
- **Health education campaigns** via mass SMS, social media and websites.
- **Programme monitoring**: immunisation, maternal and child health, TB, non-communicable diseases.
- **Supply chain**: tracking vaccines and medicines.
- **Training health workers** through e-learning and tele-mentoring.
- **Geographic information systems (GIS)**: mapping disease cases, health facilities and high-risk areas.

## 6.4 Indian eHealth examples

Facts change often; check the current status on the official MoHFW, NHM and NHA websites.

| Initiative | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| **eSanjeevani** | MoHFW's national telemedicine service: a doctor-to-doctor (hub-and-spoke) model linking Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (health and wellness centres) with specialists, and a patient-to-doctor OPD service |
| **Tele-MANAS** | National tele-mental health programme with a toll-free helpline (14416) |
| **ABDM and ABHA** | National digital health ecosystem; consent-based sharing of records (Unit 3) |
| **U-WIN** | Digital registration and tracking of routine immunisation |
| **Kilkari** | Weekly voice messages on pregnancy and child care to families' mobile phones |
| **RCH portal and ANMOL** | Name-based tracking of pregnant women and children; ANMOL is the tablet application used by ANMs |
| **Ni-kshay** | Case notification and monitoring of TB patients |
| **IHIP** | Integrated Health Information Platform for disease surveillance under IDSP |
| **HMIS portal** | Facility-wise monthly reporting of service data under NHM |

## 6.5 Benefits and challenges of eHealth

| Benefits | Challenges |
| --- | --- |
| Access for rural and remote people | **Digital divide**: no phone, internet or skills, especially among the elderly and the poor |
| Saves travel time and cost | Low **e-health literacy**; misinformation online |
| Continuity of care and follow-up | Limited physical examination in teleconsultation |
| Patient empowerment and self-care | Privacy and security of data |
| Faster specialist opinion | Network and power problems |
| Data for planning | Legal and ethical questions, unclear accountability |

**e-health literacy** is the ability to seek, find, understand and appraise health information from electronic sources and apply it. Nurses should teach patients to check the source and date of information and to discuss it with a health professional.

## 6.6 Public health informatics and the role of nurses

**Public health informatics** is the systematic application of information science and technology to public health practice, research and learning, focusing on **populations** rather than individual patients.

**Functions**: surveillance and outbreak detection; disease and immunisation registries; programme monitoring and evaluation; resource planning; health promotion; emergency response.

**Role of nurses (especially community health nurses, ANMs, CHOs)**

- Collect accurate population data (household surveys, eligible-couple registers, immunisation records) and enter it in national portals.
- Report notifiable diseases and unusual clusters promptly.
- Use data for local action: identify drop-outs from immunisation or ANC, high-risk mothers, TB patients missing treatment.
- Provide teleconsultation support at health and wellness centres.
- Teach the community to use health apps and ABHA safely.
- Protect the confidentiality of community data.

## Part B: Using information in healthcare management

## 6.7 Nursing information system (NIS)

A **nursing information system** is the part of the hospital information system that supports nursing practice, nursing administration, education and research by managing nursing data.

**Components**

| Component | Functions |
| --- | --- |
| **Clinical (patient care) component** | Admission assessment, nursing history, vital signs and charts, nursing diagnoses, care plans, nursing notes, eMAR and barcode administration, intake–output, risk scores (falls, pressure injury), patient education records, handover, discharge planning |
| **Administrative (management) component** | Staffing and scheduling, patient classification and **acuity/workload** measurement, leave and attendance, bed management, quality indicators, incident reports, supplies and inventory, budgets |
| **Education component** | Staff training records, competency checks, e-learning, policies and procedures |
| **Research component** | Data retrieval for audits and studies, nursing-sensitive outcome data |

**Characteristics of a good NIS**: easy to use, fits the nursing process, uses standard nursing terms, available at the bedside, integrated with other modules, secure, gives useful reports.

**Benefits**: less time on paperwork, legible and complete notes, fewer errors, better communication, objective staffing decisions, data showing nursing's contribution to outcomes.

## 6.8 Healthcare data for management decisions

Managers turn data into decisions through a cycle:

```text
  Collect ─► Validate/clean ─► Analyse ─► Present ─► Interpret ─► Decide ─► Act ─► Evaluate
     ▲                                                                              │
     └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Evaluation of data quality

Before using data, check that it is **accurate, complete, timely, consistent, valid and reliable**. Look for missing entries, impossible values (pulse 750) and double counting.

### Common indicators and how they are worked out

| Indicator | Formula | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Bed occupancy rate** | (Inpatient days in a period ÷ (available beds × days in the period)) × 100 | Planning beds and staff |
| **Average length of stay (ALOS)** | Inpatient days ÷ number of discharges (including deaths) | Efficiency |
| **Bed turnover rate** | Number of discharges ÷ number of beds | How often a bed is reused |
| **Nurse–patient ratio** | Nurses on duty : patients | Staffing |
| **Nursing hours per patient day** | Total nursing hours ÷ patient days | Workload |
| **Fall rate** | (Number of falls ÷ patient days) × 1000 | Safety |
| **Pressure injury incidence** | New pressure injuries ÷ patients at risk × 100 | Quality of nursing care |
| **Health care-associated infection rate** | e.g. catheter-associated UTIs per 1000 catheter days | Infection control |
| **Medication error rate** | Errors reported per 1000 doses or patient days | Safety |
| **Patient satisfaction score** | From surveys | Quality |

**Worked example**: a 30-bed ward had 810 inpatient days in a 30-day month. Bed occupancy = 810 ÷ (30 × 30) × 100 = **90%**. If there were 162 discharges, ALOS = 810 ÷ 162 = **5 days**.

### Analysis

- **Descriptive**: counts, percentages, rates, averages, trends over time.
- **Comparative**: this month vs last month, ward vs ward, our hospital vs a benchmark.
- **Statistical process control**: run charts and control charts show whether a change is real or just random variation.

### Presentation

| Method | Best for |
| --- | --- |
| Table | Exact numbers |
| Bar chart | Comparing categories (falls per ward) |
| Line graph / run chart | Trends over time (infection rate by month) |
| Pie chart | Parts of a whole (patients by diagnosis) |
| Dashboard | Several key indicators on one screen with colour codes (green/amber/red) |
| Balanced scorecard | Indicators from four views: finance, patients, internal processes, learning and growth |

### Decisions informed by data

- Staffing and rostering by acuity and census.
- Opening or closing beds; planning equipment and supplies.
- Targeting quality improvement (e.g. a rise in falls on night shift leads to more rounds and bed alarms).
- Budgeting and purchasing.
- Reporting to accreditation bodies (NABH) and government programmes.

## 6.9 Nurse manager's role

- Make sure staff enter complete, accurate data.
- Review dashboards and reports regularly and share them with staff.
- Use evidence from data, not guesswork, to justify staffing and resources.
- Protect confidentiality when presenting data (no patient names in reports).

## Remember

- eHealth = ICT for health; telemedicine = clinical care at a distance; mHealth = mobile devices.
- Telemedicine modes: synchronous, store-and-forward, remote monitoring.
- eSanjeevani = national telemedicine; Tele-MANAS = tele-mental health (14416); IHIP = surveillance; ANMOL = app for ANMs.
- Digital divide and e-health literacy are major challenges.
- Public health informatics focuses on populations; nurses collect, report and use community data.
- NIS components: clinical, administrative, education, research.
- Bed occupancy = inpatient days ÷ (beds × days) × 100; ALOS = inpatient days ÷ discharges.
- Fall rate is expressed per 1000 patient days; dashboards show key indicators at a glance.

# Unit 7: Information law and governance, healthcare quality and evidence-based practice

This notes file joins the last two INC units: **Unit IX, Information Law & Governance in Clinical Practice** (4 hours theory) and **Unit X, Healthcare Quality & Evidence Based Practice** (3 hours theory). The first part covers the ethical and legal issues of health information and of digital health in nursing, with the Indian laws and guidelines a nurse must know. The second explains how scientific evidence and informatics standards improve the quality of care.

Laws and rules change. The facts below were checked against official sources; always confirm the current position on government websites (MeitY, MoHFW, NMC, INC) before relying on them.

## Part A: Information law and governance

## 7.1 Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Privacy** | The person's right to control who collects and sees information about them |
| **Confidentiality** | The professional's duty not to disclose information shared in trust, except when allowed |
| **Security** | The technical, physical and administrative measures that protect data (passwords, encryption, locked rooms) |
| **Information governance** | The framework of policies, roles and controls that makes sure information is handled legally, securely, efficiently and ethically |
| **Data integrity** | Data are accurate and have not been changed without authority |
| **Availability** | Authorised people can get the data when they need it |

Security aims for **CIA**: Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability.

## 7.2 Ethical principles applied to health information

| Principle | Application to information |
| --- | --- |
| **Autonomy** | Patients decide who sees their data; informed consent for sharing and for telehealth |
| **Beneficence** | Use data to improve care (alerts, continuity) |
| **Non-maleficence** | Avoid harm from leaks, wrong data or wrong-patient entries |
| **Justice** | Fair access to digital services; avoid the digital divide and biased software |
| **Veracity** | Honest, accurate documentation; never alter records falsely |
| **Fidelity** | Keep promises of confidentiality |
| **Accountability** | Every entry is traceable to a user; nurses answer for what they record |

## 7.3 Ethical-legal issues in contemporary clinical practice

1. **Confidentiality breaches**: looking up records of neighbours, celebrities or colleagues without a care reason; discussing patients in lifts or on WhatsApp groups; leaving screens open.
2. **Unauthorised access and sharing of passwords**: makes it impossible to know who made an entry.
3. **Accuracy and alteration of records**: late entries must be marked as late; never delete or back-date; electronic systems keep an **audit trail**.
4. **Copy-paste documentation**: may record care that was not given, which is false documentation.
5. **Consent**: for treatment, for teleconsultation, for sharing records (ABDM consent), for photographs, for research use of data.
6. **Ownership and access**: the facility holds the record; the patient has a right to information and copies under hospital policy and the law.
7. **Retention and destruction**: records must be kept for the period required by law and policy, then destroyed securely. (The medical ethics regulations of 2002 required indoor records to be kept for 3 years; hospitals often keep them longer. Follow your hospital's policy.)
8. **Special categories**: HIV status (HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017) and mental health information (Mental Healthcare Act, 2017) carry strong confidentiality duties.
9. **Cyber-security incidents**: ransomware, phishing e-mails, lost pen drives; must be reported at once.
10. **Social media**: posting photos or details of patients, even without names, can identify them and is a breach.
11. **Electronic evidence**: electronic records can be produced as evidence in court (now under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, which replaced the Indian Evidence Act), so they must be complete and genuine.

## 7.4 Indian laws and guidelines

### Information Technology Act, 2000 (amended 2008)

The main cyber law of India. Provisions relevant to health care include:

| Section | Subject |
| --- | --- |
| 43 | Penalty and compensation for unauthorised access, damage to a computer or data |
| 43A | Compensation by a body corporate that is negligent in protecting **sensitive personal data** |
| 66 | Computer-related offences (dishonest or fraudulent acts under section 43) |
| 66C | Identity theft (misuse of passwords, electronic signatures) |
| 66E | Violation of privacy by capturing or publishing images of a person's private areas |
| 72 / 72A | Breach of confidentiality and privacy; disclosure of information in breach of a lawful contract |

The **IT (Reasonable Security Practices and Procedures and Sensitive Personal Data or Information) Rules, 2011** listed physical, physiological and mental health condition and medical records and history as sensitive personal data. When the relevant provisions of the DPDP Act are fully in force, they take over this role; check the current position.

### Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023

The **DPDP Act, 2023** received Presidential assent on **11 August 2023**. The **DPDP Rules, 2025** were notified in **November 2025**, and the duties come into force in phases. It applies to **digital** personal data (including paper data later digitised).

| Term in the Act | Meaning | Health example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Data principal** | The person the data are about (for a child or a person with a disability, includes the parent or lawful guardian) | The patient |
| **Data fiduciary** | Decides why and how data are processed | The hospital |
| **Data processor** | Processes data for a fiduciary | A software or cloud company running the HMIS |
| **Consent manager** | A registered entity through which a person can give, manage and withdraw consent | |

**Main rules**

- Process personal data only for a **lawful purpose**, with **consent** or for certain **legitimate uses**.
- Consent must be **free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous**, given by a **clear affirmative action**, preceded by a **notice** explaining what data and why, and can be **withdrawn** as easily as it was given.
- Legitimate uses without consent include responding to a **medical emergency** involving a threat to life, and measures during epidemics or disasters.
- **Children** (under 18): verifiable consent of a parent or lawful guardian is needed.
- Fiduciaries must keep data **accurate**, use **reasonable security safeguards**, **erase** data when the purpose is over (unless law requires keeping it), and report a **personal data breach** to the **Data Protection Board of India** and to each affected person.
- **Rights of the data principal**: information about processing, correction and erasure, grievance redressal, and nominating someone to act in case of death or incapacity.
- **Duties of the data principal**: no false information, no impersonation, no frivolous complaints.
- **Penalties** are monetary and can reach **₹250 crore** (the highest level, for failing to take reasonable security safeguards to prevent a breach).

**For nurses**: collect only the data needed, tell the patient why, protect devices and passwords, share only for care or with consent, and report a suspected breach to the hospital immediately.

### Telemedicine Practice Guidelines, 2020

Issued on **25 March 2020** by the Board of Governors in supersession of the Medical Council of India (with NITI Aayog), now under the National Medical Commission. They apply to **registered medical practitioners (RMPs)** and describe how teleconsultation must be done:

- **Modes**: video, audio and text (chat, e-mail, messages), each with its strengths and limits.
- **Consultations** may be patient to RMP, caregiver to RMP, **health worker to RMP** (a nurse, ANM or other health worker may connect the patient and help with the examination; the RMP remains responsible for advice), and RMP to RMP.
- Both sides must **identify** themselves: the patient's name, age and contact details; the RMP's name and registration number.
- **Consent**: implied if the patient starts the teleconsultation; **explicit** consent needed if the health worker or RMP starts it.
- The RMP decides whether teleconsultation is enough or the patient must be seen in person; **emergencies** are referred for in-person care.
- Prescribing follows medicine lists in the guidelines; certain medicines (such as narcotic and psychotropic drugs listed as prohibited) cannot be prescribed through telemedicine.
- **Records**: keep consultation records, reports and prescriptions; protect privacy and confidentiality.

### Other relevant guidance

- **INC Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct** for nurses: confidentiality, respect, accountability.
- **EHR Standards for India (2016)**: privacy, security and audit requirements for record systems.
- **ABDM Health Data Management Policy**: consent-based sharing within ABDM.

## 7.5 Ethical-legal issues in digital health applied to nursing

| Issue | Nursing implication |
| --- | --- |
| **Telenursing** | Verify patient identity; document every call; know your scope; refer when you cannot assess safely |
| **Licensure and scope** | Work only within the scope of your registration (State Nursing Council) and your institution's policy |
| **Documentation** | Electronic notes are legal records; timely, accurate, signed with your own login |
| **Consent** | Explain telehealth, recording, and data sharing in language the patient understands |
| **Use of mobile phones** | No patient photos or data on personal phones or messaging apps unless the hospital approves a secure method |
| **Decision-support software** | The nurse stays accountable even when software suggests an action |
| **Equity** | Help patients who cannot use technology; do not exclude them |
| **Professional boundaries online** | Do not "friend" patients or give advice through personal social media |

## 7.6 Elements of information governance in a hospital

- Policies on access, passwords, e-mail, internet, mobile devices and social media.
- **Role-based access** (each user sees only what the job needs) and **audit trails**.
- Staff training and signed confidentiality agreements.
- Data-sharing agreements with other organisations.
- Backup, downtime and disaster recovery plans.
- Incident reporting and breach management.
- Records retention and secure destruction schedules.

## Part B: Healthcare quality and evidence-based practice

## 7.7 Quality of health care

**Quality** is the degree to which health services increase the likelihood of desired outcomes and are consistent with current professional knowledge.

**Dimensions of quality** (Institute of Medicine): **safe, effective, patient-centred, timely, efficient and equitable**.

**Donabedian's model** evaluates quality by **structure** (staff, equipment, IT systems) → **process** (what is done: hand hygiene, timely medicines) → **outcome** (infection rates, satisfaction). Informatics supplies the data for all three.

**PDSA cycle** for improvement: **Plan** a change, **Do** it on a small scale, **Study** the data, **Act** to adopt, adapt or abandon.

## 7.8 Evidence-based practice (EBP)

**EBP** is the integration of the **best research evidence** with **clinical expertise** and **patient values and preferences** to make decisions about care (after Sackett and colleagues).

```text
          Best research evidence
                   ▲
                   │
       Clinical ───┼─── Patient values
       expertise   │    and preferences
                   ▼
           Clinical decision
     (within the available resources and context)
```

**Steps (the 5 A's)**

1. **Ask** a focused clinical question (PICO).
2. **Acquire** the evidence: search databases (PubMed, CINAHL, Cochrane).
3. **Appraise** the evidence for validity, results and relevance.
4. **Apply** it, combined with expertise and patient preferences.
5. **Assess** (evaluate) the outcome and share it.

**Levels of evidence** (highest to lowest)

```text
   1  Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs
   2  Randomised controlled trials (RCTs)
   3  Controlled trials without randomisation
   4  Cohort and case-control studies
   5  Systematic reviews of descriptive/qualitative studies
   6  Single descriptive or qualitative studies
   7  Opinion of authorities and expert committees
```

**How informatics supports EBP**: online databases and full-text journals; point-of-care references; evidence built into order sets, care plans and decision support; EHR data for audits and research; e-learning for updating knowledge.

**Barriers to EBP**: lack of time, limited access to journals, poor search and appraisal skills, resistance to change, lack of managerial support. **Facilitators**: library and internet access, journal clubs, EBP mentors, protocols that are kept up to date.

**Nursing examples**: chlorhexidine skin preparation for central lines, regular repositioning and pressure-relieving surfaces to prevent pressure injury, early mobilisation after surgery, kangaroo mother care for low-birth-weight babies.

## 7.9 Technical and professional informatics standards

| Type | Examples | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Technical standards** | HL7 v2 and FHIR, DICOM, SNOMED CT, LOINC, ICD, ISO security standards, India's EHR Standards, ABDM specifications | Make systems interoperable, safe and secure |
| **Professional standards** | Nursing informatics scope and standards of practice (American Nurses Association); TIGER informatics competencies for nurses; INC curriculum competencies; NABH standards on management of information | Define what nurses and organisations should know and do with information |

Using standards is itself evidence-based: research shows that standardised, well-designed systems reduce errors and improve outcomes, while poorly designed ones can cause harm. Health IT should therefore be **evaluated** with data before and after it is introduced.

## 7.10 Nurse's role

- Protect privacy and confidentiality in every form of record and communication.
- Follow the law and hospital policy on consent, records and telehealth.
- Base care on current evidence; question routine practices that lack evidence.
- Use quality data to improve care in your unit.

## Remember

- Privacy = patient's right; confidentiality = professional's duty; security = protective measures. CIA = confidentiality, integrity, availability.
- IT Act 2000 (amended 2008): sections 43, 43A, 66, 66C, 66E, 72, 72A.
- DPDP Act 2023: assent 11 August 2023; data principal, data fiduciary, data processor, consent manager; breach reported to the Data Protection Board; penalty up to ₹250 crore.
- Telemedicine Practice Guidelines: 25 March 2020; video, audio, text; health worker may connect patient to RMP; explicit consent if health worker or RMP starts.
- Quality dimensions: safe, effective, patient-centred, timely, efficient, equitable; Donabedian: structure–process–outcome.
- EBP = best evidence + clinical expertise + patient preferences; 5 A's: ask, acquire, appraise, apply, assess.
- Systematic reviews of RCTs are the top level of evidence; expert opinion is the lowest.
